561.title: Justified by faith (Romans 3:21–28)
561.hook: Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint declaration on justification in 1999, after centuries of argument
561.carry: all have sinned, all are loved
561.howItsDone: The Catholic Church teaches that justification is God's free gift received in baptism, which both forgives sin and renews the person within; it joined the Lutheran World Federation in the 1999 Joint Declaration, and many local parishes pray with Lutheran neighbors during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening of Romans: the gospel as the power of God. Your line was no one shut out. Did you help someone feel welcome? Day five hundred sixty-one.

October thirty-first, 1999. Augsburg, Germany. Representatives of the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation sign a document called the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification. The date is deliberate: October thirty-first is the anniversary Lutherans keep for the start of the Reformation. The city is deliberate too: Augsburg is where Lutherans set out their beliefs in 1530. For almost five centuries, this one question had divided Western Christians. And at the root of the question lay a few verses of Romans.
screen: `AUGSBURG, OCTOBER 31, 1999.` → `CATHOLICS AND LUTHERANS SIGN.` → `FIVE CENTURIES OVER A FEW VERSES.`

segments.voice: Justification translates a Greek word family built on dikaios, righteous: being made right, or set right, with God. In Romans 3, Paul has just spent two chapters showing that no one, Jew or Gentile, stands right with God by their own record. Then he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For all have sinned, and do need the glory of God." All. No exceptions, no ranking of who's worse. And in the very next breath: being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. All have sinned, and all are offered grace as a gift. A few verses later: "For we account a man to be justified by faith, without the works of the law." When Martin Luther translated that verse into German and added a word: allein, alone. Justified by faith alone. That word became a battle line. Lutherans stressed that God declares sinners righteous by grace through faith, not by anything they earn. The Council of Trent, for Catholics, stressed that God's grace truly makes a person righteous within, and that faith works through love. Each side heard the other as denying something essential. The 1999 declaration didn't erase every difference. But both churches stated together that by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work, and not because of any merit of ours, we are accepted by God and receive the Holy Spirit, who renews our hearts and calls us to good works. And they said the old condemnations no longer apply to the teaching as each side now explains it. Later, Methodists, Reformed and Anglican churches joined or welcomed it.
screen: `DIKAIOS: SET RIGHT WITH GOD.` · `ALL HAVE SINNED.` · `JUSTIFIED FREELY BY HIS GRACE.` · `LUTHER'S ALLEIN, TRENT'S ANSWER.` · then, large: `A SHARED STATEMENT, 1999.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Lutheran neighbors, or simply hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. Maybe there's a Lutheran church you drive past, or a Lutheran friend, coworker or in-law. Picture them. Remember that for centuries, people on both sides were taught to see each other as wrong about the most important thing. And remember Augsburg, where both signed the same words about grace. If you pray, you can ask blessing on that church and those people by name. If not, just wish them well, sincerely. The bell holds the time.
Justification. Being set right with God, freely, by grace: the word that divided Catholics and Lutherans for centuries, and that they spoke together in 1999. Today's word.
Your line: all have sinned, all are loved. Today, when you're tempted to rank someone as worse than you, remember the word all. Day five hundred sixty-one.

it stated a shared understanding of the basics and lifted old condemnations, but differences remain.
Luther added the word alone to Romans 3:28 in German

fork.setup: you're part of a dialogue between two churches that have condemned each other's teaching for centuries. what do you aim for?
options: get the other side to admit it was wrong.

fork.reveal: the joint declaration states a shared understanding of grace and faith, says the old condemnations don't apply to the teaching as now explained, and is honest that differences remain.

original.note: Greek: righteousness, justice, being right with God. justification comes from the same family.

trapdoor: what you thought: a technical word theologians argue about.
what it means: how anyone is set right with God: all have sinned, and grace is a free gift. Catholics and Lutherans now say much of this together.

what a scholar hears: dikaioō can mean to declare righteous or to make righteous, and that difference shaped the dispute. Luther's allein in Romans 3:28 has no word in the Greek, though he defended it as the sense.

sources.ref: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999), §15

562.title: Love poured out (Romans 5:5–8)
562.hook: the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts, while we were yet sinners
562.howItsDone: Catholics speak of grace as God's free gift, poured into the soul at baptism, and Romans 5 is among the readings the Church offers for confirmation, when it prays for the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, justification, and the declaration signed in Augsburg. Your line was all have sinned, all are loved. Did you catch yourself ranking anyone? Day five hundred sixty-two.

Would you die for a stranger? Most of us hope we'd be brave, but we don't really know. Would you die for a good person, someone kind, someone you admire? Maybe. Paul thinks about this out loud in Romans 5, almost like a man doing math on a napkin. And then he lands on something that doesn't add up at all: someone who died for people who weren't good, and weren't his friends yet.
screen: `WOULD YOU DIE FOR A STRANGER?` → `FOR A GOOD PERSON, MAYBE.` → `THE MATH THAT DOESN'T ADD UP.`

segments.voice: Start with the image in verse five. In the Douay-Rheims: "the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts, by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us." Charity is the old English word for love, the Latin caritas, the Greek agape. And it's poured. Not measured out in spoonfuls, not earned drop by drop. Poured, like water from a jug, until it runs over. Paul says this is why hope doesn't disappoint: the love is already inside, given. Then the napkin math. Scarcely, he says, would anyone die for a righteous man; maybe for a good man someone might dare to die. But then, in the Douay-Rheims: "God commendeth his charity towards us; because when as yet we were sinners, according to the time, Christ died for us." When as yet we were sinners: or, in the older English many people know, while we were yet sinners. Not after we cleaned up. Not once we deserved it. While we were still a mess, still far off, still not his friends. That's the order Paul insists on: love first, then change. Not change first, then love. Catholics speak of this as grace, a gift given before any merit, and the Catechism quotes verse five when it calls love the Holy Spirit's first gift. Notice what it does to the way you look in the mirror. Your worst day was not a day you were unloved. And notice what it does to how you look at other people: no one you meet is outside the reach of while we were yet sinners. The love came first. That's the whole point of the word poured.
screen: `CARITAS, AGAPE: LOVE.` · `POURED, NOT MEASURED.` · `SCARCELY FOR A RIGHTEOUS MAN.` · `WHILE WE WERE YET SINNERS.` · then, large: `LOVE FIRST, THEN CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive love you didn't earn. This one is harder than it sounds. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time someone was kind to you when you didn't deserve it. A parent after you'd slammed a door. A friend after you'd let them down. A stranger on a bad day. Let yourself remember it fully, without explaining it away. Then imagine love being poured out, like water, on you exactly as you are right now. Don't fix anything first. Just receive. If you pray, you can simply say thank you. The bell holds the time.
Poured. Not measured in spoonfuls but poured out, like water from a jug, until it runs over: God's charity in our hearts. Today's word.
Your line: while we were yet sinners. Today, be kind to one person before they've earned it. Day five hundred sixty-two.

help them now.

fork.reveal: not graded. but the pattern Paul describes is love first, while we were yet sinners, and change afterward.

trapdoor: what you thought: God loves good people.
what it means: God's love was poured out first, while we were still sinners, not as a reward for becoming good.
what a scholar hears: the verb ekkechutai, poured out, is a perfect tense: it has been poured, and it remains. the same verb is used of the Spirit poured out at Pentecost in Acts 2.

563.title: Buried with him (Romans 6:3–4)
563.hook: baptized into his death to walk in newness of life
563.howItsDone: Catholics bless themselves with holy water as they enter a church, recalling their baptism, and Romans 6:3–11 is the Epistle read at the Easter Vigil, the night new members are baptized.

segments.voice: Yesterday, love poured out before we deserved it. Your line was while we were yet sinners. Were you kind to someone before they earned it? Day five hundred sixty-three.

In some old churches, the baptismal font isn't a basin. It's a pool, set into the floor, with steps going down one side and up the other. Some are even shaped like a tomb, or a cross. You walk down into the water, you go under, and you come up the other side. Nobody designed that by accident. The shape is a sermon in stone, and the sermon comes from two verses in Romans 6.
screen: `A FONT WITH STEPS DOWN.` → `SHAPED LIKE A TOMB.` → `A SERMON IN STONE.`

segments.voice: Paul has just said that where sin abounded, grace abounded more. Someone might take that and say: great, then let's keep sinning so there's more grace. Paul's answer is, God forbid. And then he asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Know you not that all we, who are baptized in Christ Jesus, are baptized in his death?" The Greek word baptizo means to dip or plunge, to immerse. Paul sees baptism as a plunge into Christ's own death and burial. Then verse four: "For we are buried together with him by baptism into death; that as Christ is risen from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also may walk in newness of life." Buried with him. The old self goes down into the water the way a body goes into a grave. And just as Christ came up from the tomb, the baptized come up to walk, step by step, in a life that's new. Not a fresh coat of paint on the old life. A new one. It's why the Church baptizes new members at the Easter Vigil, the night between Christ's burial and his rising. It's why the newly baptized are handed a candle lit from the Easter candle. And it's why there are fonts with steps down and steps up. Whether a person is immersed in a pool or has water poured on the head, Catholics believe the same thing happens: dying and rising with Christ. Someone baptized as an infant doesn't remember it. Paul writes as though it shapes every step after: walk in newness of life.
screen: `SHALL WE SIN THAT GRACE MAY ABOUND?` · `BAPTIZO: TO PLUNGE.` · `BURIED WITH HIM.` · `RAISED UP, TO WALK.` · then, large: `NEWNESS OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless yourself with water. If you're near a church, holy water is by the door. If not, any water will do as a reminder: the kitchen tap, a glass, a bathroom sink. Settle, and breathe. Touch the water with your fingers. Catholics make the sign of the cross with it, remembering their baptism. If that's not your practice, just feel the cool of it and think of one old habit you'd like to leave in the water, and one step of new life you'd like to take today. Let the water dry on your skin. The bell holds the time.
Baptizo. The Greek word for plunge or immerse: Paul's picture of baptism as a burial with Christ, and a rising to newness of life. Today's word.
Your line: newness of life. Today, every time you wash your hands, remember one thing you've left behind. Day five hundred sixty-three.

564.title: The good I would (Romans 7:15–25)
564.hook: Paul admits he does what he hates
564.howItsDone: Catholics bring the struggle Paul describes to the sacrament of reconciliation, naming their sins to a priest and receiving absolution, and some make a nightly examination of conscience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptizo: buried with him in baptism. Your line was newness of life. What did you leave in the water? Day five hundred sixty-four.

January first: a resolution on a sticky note. No more scrolling in bed. January third, one in the morning: a phone glowing in the dark, the sticky note still on the mirror. The gap between what a person means to do and what they actually do is an old one. Paul's letters can sound lofty and sure of themselves. Chapter seven of Romans does not. In it, Paul describes that gap in the first person, with no excuses.
screen: `JANUARY FIRST: A RESOLUTION.` → `JANUARY THIRD, 1 A.M.` → `PAUL NAMES THE GAP.`

segments.voice: In Romans 7, Paul writes, in the Douay-Rheims: "For that which I work, I understand not. For I do not that good which I will; but the evil which I hate, that I do." A few lines later he says it again, almost like a man pacing a room: "For the good which I will, I do not; but the evil which I will not, that I do." Older English put it as the good I would: would in the old sense of what I want, what I will. He agrees the law is good. He wants the good. And something in him pulls the other way. He calls it sin dwelling in me, a different law at war in his members. And then the cry: "Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" That's not a theologian's polished sentence. It's a groan. But it doesn't end there. The very next line answers: "The grace of God, by Jesus Christ our Lord." The Greek reads, thanks be to God. Either way, the answer isn't a better resolution. It's a person. Now, honesty: readers have argued for centuries about who the I in this chapter is. Some, including Saint Augustine in his later writings, read it as Paul describing his life as a believer, still struggling. Others read it as Paul looking back at life before Christ, or speaking for humanity in Adam's shoes. The Church hasn't required one reading. What Catholics do recognize here is something the tradition calls concupiscence: an inclination toward sin that remains even after baptism, not itself sin, but the place where the struggle happens. Paul doesn't hide it. He names the divided heart, and then he points to grace.
screen: `THE GOOD WHICH I WILL, I DO NOT.` · `A LAW AT WAR IN MY MEMBERS.` · `UNHAPPY MAN THAT I AM.` · `WHO IS THE I?` · then, large: `THE GRACE OF GOD, BY JESUS CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be honest about your divided heart. Settle, and breathe. Name, silently, one thing you keep doing that you don't want to do. Not ten things. One. Don't argue with yourself, don't make a plan yet. Just let it be true, the way Paul let it be true on the page. Notice that naming it is already different from hiding it. Then, if you pray, you can borrow Paul's own words: who shall deliver me, and, the grace of God, by Jesus Christ. If you don't, simply breathe out, and let the honesty be enough for today. The bell holds the time.
Wretched. Paul's own word for himself in Romans seven, unhappy man that I am, caught between the good he wills and the evil he does. Today's word.
Your line: who shall deliver me. Today, when you catch yourself in the gap, don't hide it: name it, and ask for help. Day five hundred sixty-four.

565.title: The Spirit prays (Romans 8:26–27)
565.hook: we don't know how to pray, and the Spirit asks for us with groanings
565.howItsDone: Catholics often begin prayer by asking the Holy Spirit's help, and the Church teaches that the Spirit is the interior teacher of prayer; some pray in silence, without words, before the Blessed Sacrament.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wretched: the good I would, and the evil I would not. Your line was who shall deliver me. Did you name the gap honestly? Day five hundred sixty-five.

A hospital waiting room at three in the morning. A woman sits with her coat still on; her husband is in surgery. She wants to pray and has no idea what to say. Heal him? Give me strength? Let it be quick? Nothing she knows by heart seems to fit. The words won't come. All she has is a long breath out. Paul wrote about a moment like that, and he didn't call it a failure.
screen: `A WAITING ROOM, 3 A.M.` → `NO WORDS COME.` → `ONLY A LONG BREATH OUT.`

segments.voice: After chapter seven's cry, who shall deliver me, chapter eight opens with no condemnation, and then it is full of the Spirit. Paul has just said that all creation groans, like a woman in labor, waiting. We groan too, he says, waiting. Then this, in the Douay-Rheims: "Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmity. For we know not what we should pray for as we ought; but the Spirit himself asketh for us with unspeakable groanings." Notice three things. First, Paul includes himself: we know not what to pray for. The apostle whose name is on so many New Testament letters admits he doesn't always know how to pray. Second, the Spirit helps our infirmity, our weakness. The Greek verb pictures someone taking hold of the other end of a heavy load. In Paul's picture, the one who prays isn't carrying it alone. Third, unspeakable groanings. Too deep for words. The Spirit's own prayer sounds less like a speech and more like a sigh. And the next verse adds that God, who searches hearts, knows what the Spirit means, because the Spirit asks according to God's will. So, on Paul's reading, the wordless sigh in the waiting room is not a failed prayer. It's a prayer the Spirit carries. The Catechism quotes this passage when it calls the Holy Spirit the interior master of Christian prayer.
screen: `CREATION GROANS, AND SO DO WE.` · `WE KNOW NOT WHAT TO PRAY FOR.` · `THE SPIRIT TAKES THE OTHER END.` · `UNSPEAKABLE GROANINGS.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT PRAYS FOR US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sigh as a prayer. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind whatever is heaviest right now, something you don't know how to pray about. Don't look for words. Breathe in slowly, and then let out a long sigh, out loud if you can. Let that sigh carry the whole thing. Do it again. If you pray, you can rest in Paul's picture: the Spirit asking, in that breath, what you can't. If you don't, just notice how much a sigh can hold. Then rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Groanings. What the Spirit prays in us when we don't know how, too deep for words, carrying the other end of the load. Today's word.
Your line: the spirit prays for us. Today, when words run out, let one long sigh be your prayer. Day five hundred sixty-five.

566.title: All things work together (Romans 8:28)
566.hook: to them that love God all things work together unto good
566.howItsDone: Catholics speak of divine providence, God's care that guides all things toward good without causing evil, and some offer up their sufferings, uniting them with Christ's, trusting God to bring good from them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, groanings: the Spirit praying in us with sighs too deep for words. Your line was the spirit prays for us. Did a sigh become a prayer? Day five hundred sixty-six.

It's printed on mugs and greeting cards. People say it at funerals, sometimes kindly, sometimes too fast. Everything happens for a reason. It's usually meant well. And on a terrible day, it can land like a slap. Some who say it think they're quoting the Bible. So it's worth looking carefully at the verse it's often borrowed from, because what Paul actually says is both stronger and more careful than the greeting card.
screen: `ON MUGS AND GREETING CARDS.` → `EVERYTHING HAPPENS FOR A REASON?` → `WHAT PAUL ACTUALLY SAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the Douay-Rheims: "And we know that to them that love God, all things work together unto good, to such as, according to his purpose, are called to be saints." Notice first what it doesn't say. It doesn't say all things are good. Paul has just been talking about groaning, suffering, and a creation in labor pains. In the next verses he'll list tribulation, famine, the sword. He knows terrible things are terrible. Second, notice the verb: work together. The Greek is sunergei, works together. Not each thing is good on its own, but all things, woven together, are made to serve good. Third, notice who's doing the weaving. Paul's point is that the good isn't automatic, like fate. It comes from someone: the God whose Spirit, Paul said two verses earlier, prays in us. And fourth, the good Paul means is bigger than comfort. The next verse says it plainly: to be conformed to the image of his Son. Becoming like Christ. Paul doesn't offer the verse as an explanation of why the bad thing happened. And he never says the reason will be visible. He says, we know.
screen: `NOT: ALL THINGS ARE GOOD.` · `SUNERGEI: WORKING TOGETHER.` · `GOD IS THE ONE WHO WEAVES.` · `THE GOOD: BECOMING LIKE CHRIST.` · then, large: `ALL THINGS WORK TOGETHER UNTO GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for good in a setback. Gently. Settle, and breathe. Choose a setback from your past, not your deepest wound, just something that went wrong. A job you didn't get. A move you didn't want. A plan that fell apart. Look at it from here. Was anything woven out of it, a friendship, a strength, a patience, a direction you wouldn't have found? If you find something, let yourself be grateful. If you don't, that's honest too; Paul says we know, not that we see. If you pray, you can hand God what you can't make sense of yet. The bell holds the time.
Sunergei. Paul's word, works together: not everything is good alone, but God weaves all things toward good for those who love him. Today's word.
Your line: all things. Today, when something goes wrong, skip the greeting card, and just ask what might be woven from it. Day five hundred sixty-six.

567.title: Nothing shall separate (Romans 8:35–39)
567.hook: neither death nor life nor angels nor height nor depth
567.howItsDone: Romans 8:31–39 is one of the readings the Church offers for Catholic funeral Masses, and many Catholics keep these verses close in illness and grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sunergei, not the greeting-card version. Your line was all things. What might be woven from a setback? Day five hundred sixty-seven.

Make a list of the things you're most afraid of. Be honest. Losing someone. Getting sick. Being alone. Money running out. Something you did coming to light. Dying. Most of us carry a list like that somewhere below the surface, and it gets louder at night. Paul made one too, at the end of Romans 8. And then he did something unexpected with it. He put the word nothing in front of it.
screen: `A LIST OF YOUR FEARS.` → `PAUL MADE ONE TOO.` → `THEN HE WROTE: NOTHING.`

segments.voice: First, Paul asks the question, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation? or distress? or famine? or nakedness? or danger? or persecution? or the sword?" Those weren't abstractions for Paul. He'd been shipwrecked, beaten with rods, hungry, cold, in danger from rivers and robbers, and tradition says he'd die by the sword in Rome. Then he answers: "But in all these things we overcome, because of him that hath loved us." And then the great list: "For I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor might, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Listen to how he builds it. Mostly in pairs: death and life, angels and principalities, things present and things to come, height and depth. He's covering everything: every moment of time, every corner of space, every power seen and unseen. And just in case he missed something, nor any other creature. Anything that was made. I am sure, he says. Not I hope, not I feel. Convinced. Notice what he doesn't promise. He doesn't say none of these things will happen. Famine and sword might come. He says none of them can cut the thread between you and the love of God. The Church reads this passage at many funerals, because it reaches even past death. And it ends this great chapter that began with no condemnation. From no condemnation to no separation.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your fear, and add nothing separates. Settle, and breathe. Pick one fear from your list. Say it to yourself plainly: losing my job. My diagnosis. My kid's future. Then, after it, in the same breath, add Paul's words: nothing shall separate us. Not as a magic spell that makes the fear go away, but as a sentence put next to it. Do it with a second fear if you like. If you pray, you can rest in the love of God that Paul was sure of. If not, notice what it's like to set a fear beside a promise. The bell holds the time.
Separate. The Greek word behind Paul's great list: nothing in time or space can separate us from the love of God. Today's word.

Your line: nothing shall separate us. Today, when a fear rises, add those words. And that's week eighty-one: justification, poured, buried with him, wretched, the Spirit prays, sunergei, and nothing shall separate. Day five hundred sixty-seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: a comforting verse for hard times.
what it means: Paul names every power of time, space and creation, and says none can cut us off from the love of God in Christ.
what a scholar hears: height and depth may echo astrological terms for the heavens, which ancient people feared ruled their fate. Paul places even these under nothing.
